questions.question: What is the remainder when 17 is divided by 5?
questions.explanation: 17 = 3·5 + 2, so 17 mod 5 = 2. This is the everyday meaning of modulo.

questions.question: Which set of integers does `Z/12Z` represent?
options: All integers from −12 to 12 inclusive
The set {0, 1, 2, …, 11} under arithmetic mod 12
All multiples of 12 starting from 0 upward
The set {1, 2, 3, …, 12} under arithmetic mod 12
questions.explanation: Z/nZ denotes integers reduced mod n, giving residues {0, 1, …, n−1}. For n = 12 you get the 12-hour clock face.

questions.question: When does `a ≡ b (mod n)` hold?
options: When a equals b after both wrap around n once
When n divides the difference (a − b)
When a and b have the same number of digits modulo n
When n divides the product (a · b) exactly
questions.explanation: Definition: a ≡ b (mod n) iff n | (a − b). Equivalently, a and b leave the same remainder when divided by n.

questions.question: Which structure does `Z/nZ` form when n is prime?
options: A commutative ring where no element has an inverse
A field where every non-zero element has an inverse
A multiplicative group that includes zero as identity
A monoid under addition with no multiplication defined
questions.explanation: When n = p is prime, every non-zero element of Z/pZ has a multiplicative inverse, making it the finite field F_p (also written GF(p)).

questions.question: Why can you reduce mod n during a long modular computation instead of waiting until the end?
options: Because addition is associative on integers in general
Because reduction mod n is a homomorphism from Z to Z/nZ
Because Python's `%` operator returns non-negative results
Because all integers must fit into a 64-bit register
questions.explanation: Reduction is a ring homomorphism, so it commutes with +, −, ·. Reducing intermediates keeps numbers small without changing the final result.

questions.question: When does `a` have a multiplicative inverse modulo n?
options: Always, provided a is strictly greater than zero
When gcd(a, n) equals 1, i.e. a and n are coprime
When a is strictly less than n and divides n exactly
When n is composite and a is itself a prime number
questions.explanation: a⁻¹ mod n exists iff gcd(a, n) = 1. The Extended Euclidean Algorithm (lesson 2) computes it.

questions.question: Two parties encrypt the same m with RSA using the same modulus n but different exponents e1, e2 (gcd(e1, e2) = 1). What can an attacker who captures c1, c2 recover?
options: Nothing — RSA security holds even with a shared modulus n
Only the public exponents e1, e2 via Fermat factoring on n
The plaintext m, via Bezout coefficients s·e1 + t·e2 = 1
The private key d, via Wiener's continued-fraction attack
questions.explanation: Common-modulus attack. Find s, t with s·e1 + t·e2 = 1 via extended Euclid, then c1^s · c2^t ≡ m^1 ≡ m (mod n). Never reuse n across users in textbook RSA.
